### 1. Reformulation as a variational inequality

Set

$$a(u,v)=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx,\qquad \ell(v)=\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,v\,d\Sigma-\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,v\,d\Sigma,$$

so that $J(v)=\tfrac12 a(v,v)-\ell(v)$. The admissible set

$$V^{+}(\Omega)=\bigl\{v\in H^{1}(\Omega):v|_{\Sigma_3}\ge 0\bigr\}$$

is a **closed convex cone** in $H^{1}(\Omega)$ (closed by the continuity of the trace map $H^{1}(\Omega)\to L^{2}(\partial\Omega)$; a cone because $v\ge0\Rightarrow\lambda v\ge0$ for $\lambda\ge0$).

Since $J$ is quadratic with positive-semidefinite Hessian $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, it is convex. A convex differentiable functional on a closed convex set is minimized at $u\in V^{+}$ **iff** the first-order variational inequality holds:

$$\boxed{\;a(u,v-u)\ge\ell(v-u)\quad\forall\,v\in V^{+}(\Omega)\;}$$

i.e.

$$\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla(v-u)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}(v-u)\,d\Sigma-\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}(v-u)\,d\Sigma,\qquad\forall\,v\in V^{+}. \tag{VI}$$

---

### 2. Existence (direct method)

**Power-balance (solvability) condition.** For any constant $c\ge0$ we have $c\in V^{+}$ and $J(c)=c\bigl(-\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,d\Sigma+\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\Sigma\bigr)$. Hence a necessary condition for $J$ to be bounded below on $V^{+}$ is

$$\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\Sigma\;\ge\;\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,d\Sigma. \tag{PB}$$

Physically: the total heat-removal capacity of the heatpipe saddle must be at least the total injected power.

**Coercivity under (PB).** Decompose $v=\bar v + v_0$ with $\bar v=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega v$ and $\int_\Omega v_0=0$. By Poincaré–Wirtinger, $\|v_0\|_{H^1}\le C\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$. On $V^+$ the constant part is controlled: if (PB) holds with strict inequality, $J(v)\to+\infty$ as $\|v\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ because the gradient term $\tfrac12\|\nabla v\|^2$ dominates the linear part on $v_0$ (by Poincaré) while the constant part contributes $\bar v\bigl(\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}-\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr)\ge0$ for $\bar v\ge0$ (and $\bar v<0$ is excluded on the active part of $\Sigma_3$ where $v=0$). If (PB) holds with equality, the constant is a flat direction but $V^+\ni v\mapsto J(v)$ is still weakly l.s.c. and bounded below; a minimizer exists (possibly a family differing by a non-negative constant).

By the **direct method of the calculus of variations**: $V^+$ is closed convex (hence weakly closed), $J$ is weakly sequentially l.s.c. (the quadratic part by Rellich compactness of the trace, the linear part is continuous), and coercive under (PB). Therefore:

> **Theorem (Existence).** If (PB) holds, $J$ attains its minimum on $V^{+}(\Omega)$.

---

### 3. Strong form: PDE, boundary conditions, and complementarity

Write $\partial\Omega=\Sigma_1\cup\Sigma_2\cup\Sigma_3$ (disjoint, up to measure-zero edges), where $\Sigma_2$ denotes any remaining boundary portion (insulated surfaces, symmetry axis of the volume of revolution, etc.). Insert $w=v-u$ into (VI) and integrate by parts:

$$\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla w\,dx=-\int_\Omega(\Delta u)\,w\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\,w\,d\Sigma.$$

Since $w=v-u$ is **unconstrained** on $\Sigma_1$ and $\Sigma_2$ (the constraint $v\ge0$ acts only on $\Sigma_3$), the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations applied to (VI) yields, pointwise a.e.:

| Region | Condition | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| $\Omega$ | $-\Delta u=0$ | bulk term vanishes for all $w$ |
| $\Sigma_1$ | $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}=q_{\mathrm{in}}$ | Neumann (prescribed inward flux) |
| $\Sigma_2$ | $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}=0$ | natural/homogeneous Neumann (insulated or symmetry) |
| $\Sigma_3$ | see below | inequality constraint |

**Complementarity system on $\Sigma_3$.** On $\Sigma_3$ the inequality (VI) reduces to

$$\int_{\Sigma_3}\Bigl(\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}+q_{\mathrm{out}}\Bigr)(v-u)\,d\Sigma\;\ge\;0\qquad\forall\,v\ge0\text{ on }\Sigma_3,\quad u\ge0\text{ on }\Sigma_3.$$

This is a variational inequality on the cone $\{w\in H^{1/2}(\Sigma_3):w\ge0\}$, equivalent (by the standard pointwise characterization of such VIs) to the **three conditions**

$$\boxed{\begin{cases} u\ge 0 & \text{on }\Sigma_3,\\[4pt] \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}+q_{\mathrm{out}}\ge 0 & \text{on }\Sigma_3,\\[4pt] u\Bigl(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}+q_{\mathrm{out}}\Bigr)=0 & \text{on }\Sigma_3. \end{cases}}\tag{CS}$$

**Physical reading.** With $\mathbf{q}=-\nabla u$ (Fourier's law), the outward heat flux through $\Sigma_3$ is $-\partial u/\partial n$. Condition (CS) says:

- $u\ge0$: temperature at the heatpipe interface never drops below the reference (taken as $0$).
- $-\partial u/\partial n\le q_{\mathrm{out}}$: the outward flux never exceeds the heatpipe capacity $q_{\mathrm{out}}$.
- **Complementarity**: wherever $u>0$ (interface above reference temperature) the heatpipe operates at full capacity, $\partial u/\partial n=-q_{\mathrm{out}}$; wherever $u=0$ (interface at reference temperature) the flux is at or below capacity, $\partial u/\partial n\ge-q_{\mathrm{out}}$.

The set $\Gamma_0:=\{x\in\Sigma_3:u(x)=0\}$ is the **inactive (saturated) contact region**, and $\Gamma_+:=\{x\in\Sigma_3:u(x)>0\}$ is the **active region**. Their partition is determined as part of the solution — this is a **free-boundary problem**.

---

### 4. Uniqueness

Let $u_1,u_2\in V^+$ both satisfy (VI). Setting $v=u_2$ in the VI for $u_1$ and $v=u_1$ in the VI for $u_2$, then adding:

$$a(u_1-u_2,\,u_2-u_1)\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad a(u_2-u_1,\,u_1-u_2)\ge0\;\Longrightarrow\;a(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)\le0.$$

Since $a(w,w)=\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}^2\ge0$, we get $\nabla(u_1-u_2)=0$, hence $u_1-u_2\equiv c$ (constant).

- **If the inactive set $\Gamma_0$ has positive measure:** $u_1=0=u_2$ on $\Gamma_0$ forces $c=0$, so $u_1=u_2$ — **unique minimizer**.
- **If $\Gamma_0=\emptyset$ (constraint inactive everywhere, $u>0$ on all of $\Sigma_3$):** (CS) gives $\partial u/\partial n=-q_{\mathrm{out}}$ on all of $\Sigma_3$, reducing to a pure Neumann problem. The minimizer is **unique up to an additive constant** (the temperature reference level), and (PB) must hold with equality for consistency ($\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}=\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}$).

---

### 5. Axisymmetric reduction (volume of revolution)

Since $\Omega$ is a volume of revolution about an axis (say the $z$-axis) and the data $q_{\mathrm{in}}$ (uniform on $\Sigma_1$) and $q_{\mathrm{out}}$ (on $\Sigma_3$) are axisymmetric, the solution is axisymmetric by uniqueness: $u=u(r,z)$. In cylindrical coordinates the Laplace equation becomes

$$-\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\Bigl(r\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\Bigr)-\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2}=0\quad\text{in }\omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2,$$

where $\omega$ is the meridional cross-section, with the regularity condition $\partial u/\partial r=0$ on the symmetry axis $r=0$ (absorbed into $\Sigma_2$), the Neumann condition $\partial u/\partial n=q_{\mathrm{in}}$ on the meridional image of $\Sigma_1$, and the complementarity system (CS) on the meridional image of $\Sigma_3$. The boundary integrals acquire the weight $2\pi r$.

---

### Summary

The minimizer of $J$ over $V^{+}(\Omega)$ is the unique (up to an additive constant when the constraint is everywhere inactive) function $u\in H^{1}(\Omega)$ satisfying the **harmonic equation with mixed Neumann–complementarity boundary conditions**:

$$\begin{cases}
-\Delta u=0 & \text{in }\Omega,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}=q_{\mathrm{in}} & \text{on }\Sigma_1,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}=0 & \text{on }\Sigma_2,\\[6pt]
u\ge0,\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}+q_{\mathrm{out}}\ge0,\quad u\Bigl(\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial n}+q_{\mathrm{out}}\Bigr)=0 & \text{on }\Sigma_3,
\end{cases}$$

equivalently characterized by the variational inequality (VI) on the closed convex cone $V^{+}(\Omega)$. Existence requires the global power-balance condition $\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\Sigma\ge\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,d\Sigma$. The complementarity on $\Sigma_3$ makes the problem a **free-boundary problem**: the partition of $\Sigma_3$ into the active region (full heatpipe flux, $u>0$) and the inactive region (sub-capacity flux, $u=0$) is unknown a priori and emerges from the solution.

is a **closed convex cone** in $H^{1}(\Omega)$ (closed by the continuity of the trace map $H^{1}(\Omega)\to L^{2}(\partial\Omega)$; a cone because $v\ge0\Rightarrow\lambda v\ge0$ for $\lambda\ge0$).

Since $J$ is quadratic with positive-semidefinite Hessian $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, it is convex. A convex differentiable functional on a closed convex set is minimized at $u\in V^{+}$ **iff** the first-order variational inequality holds:

$$\boxed{\;a(u,v-u)\ge\ell(v-u)\quad\forall\,v\in V^{+}(\Omega)\;}$$

i.e.

$$\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla(v-u)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}(v-u)\,d\Sigma-\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}(v-u)\,d\Sigma,\qquad\forall\,v\in V^{+}. \tag{VI}$$

---

### 2. Existence (direct method)

**Power-balance (solvability) condition.** For any constant $c\ge0$ we have $c\in V^{+}$ and $J(c)=c\bigl(-\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,d\Sigma+\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\Sigma\bigr)$. Hence a necessary condition for $J$ to be bounded below on $V^{+}$ is

$$\int_{\Sigma_3}q_{\mathrm{out}}\,d\Sigma\;\ge\;\int_{\Sigma_1}q_{\mathrm{in}}\,d\Sigma. \tag{PB}$$

Physically: the total heat-removal capacity of the heatpipe saddle must be at least the total injected power.

**Coercivity under (PB).** Decompose $v=\bar v + v_0$ with $\bar v=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega v$ and $\int_\Omega v_0=0$. By Poincaré–Wirtinger, $\|v_0\|_{H^1}\le C\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$.
